subject: Chemistry
description: Substitution, addition, elimination, oxidation, esterification, common conversions

questions.stem: An ALKANE reacting with halogen in presence of UV light undergoes:
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated → cannot undergo addition. With X₂ + UV → SUBSTITUTION (free-radical, chain mechanism: initiation, propagation, termination). CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, then → CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄. Mixture of products. Addition reactions belong to alkenes/alkynes (e.g., CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br). Elimination — opposite of addition; commonly E1/E2 dehydrohalogenation.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Ethylene (CH₂=CH₂) reacts with Br₂ to form 1,2-dibromoethane. This is an example of:

options.option_text: Electrophilic addition across the C=C double bond

questions.explanation: Alkenes (C=C) — π bond — undergo ADDITION reactions. With Br₂: orange Br₂ → colourless. The 'bromine water test' decolourises with alkene. Markovnikov's rule (asymmetric reagents like HBr): H attaches to the C with more H's already (i.e., adds H to C with most H — 'rich gets richer'). Anti-Markovnikov with peroxides (radical mechanism). Other addition reactions: hydrogenation (H₂ + Ni catalyst), hydration (H₂O + acid → alcohol), HCl addition, hydroboration-oxidation.

questions.stem: When ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170 °C, the product is:
questions.explanation: C₂H₅OH at 170 °C with conc H₂SO₄ → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. Acid-catalysed DEHYDRATION (an elimination reaction; intramolecular). At 140 °C, two ethanol molecules can dehydrate INTER-molecularly to give diethyl ether: 2 C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅-O-C₂H₅ + H₂O. With acidified KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₇ → ethanol oxidises to acetaldehyde (mild) → acetic acid (strong). Distinct mechanisms based on conditions.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid (with acid catalyst) producing an ester + water is called:
questions.explanation: Fischer Esterification: R-COOH + R'-OH ⇌ R-COO-R' + H₂O (H₂SO₄ catalyst, heat). Reversible. Le Chatelier — shift right by removing water (Dean-Stark trap) or excess alcohol. Used industrially for fragrances, plasticisers (DEHP, DBP). Saponification — opposite-direction (with NaOH instead of acid): ester + NaOH → carboxylate salt (soap) + alcohol. Hydrolysis (acidic) — ester + water → acid + alcohol.

questions.stem: Vegetable oils (liquid at room temperature) are converted to vanaspati / dalda (semi-solid) by:

options.option_text: Hydrogenation — addition of H₂ across C=C double bonds with Ni catalyst

questions.explanation: Vegetable oils — unsaturated triglycerides (multiple C=C). Hydrogenation: H₂ + Ni catalyst (~150 °C, 5 atm) → saturates double bonds → solidifies the fat. Industrial process used to make vanaspati ghee from groundnut/cottonseed/soybean oil. Concern: PARTIAL hydrogenation creates 'trans-fats' (cis isomer flips to trans during reaction), which raise LDL cholesterol, lower HDL → cardiovascular risk. FSSAI capped trans-fat in PHVOs (partially hydrogenated vegetable oils) to ≤ 2% by 1 January 2022.

questions.explanation: Polyethene = (-CH₂-CH₂-)ₙ — repeated ethylene units join via ADDITION polymerisation; no byproduct (every atom of monomer ends up in polymer). Initiated by free radicals (peroxides), Ziegler-Natta catalyst (Ti/Al), or metallocene catalyst. CONDENSATION polymerisation — releases small byproducts (water, HCl) — e.g., nylon, polyester (PET), Bakelite, urea-formaldehyde. Other addition polymers — PVC (vinyl chloride), polypropylene, PTFE (Teflon), polystyrene, neoprene rubber, polyacrylonitrile.

questions.stem: When ethanol is OXIDISED with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange) or KMnO₄ (purple), the colour:

options.option_text: Changes (orange → green for K₂Cr₂O₇; purple → colourless for KMnO₄) as oxidation proceeds

questions.explanation: K₂Cr₂O₇ — Cr(VI) orange → Cr(III) green during reduction. KMnO₄ — Mn(VII) purple → Mn(II) colourless. Ethanol gets oxidised: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde) → CH₃COOH (acetic acid). Useful tests in qualitative organic chemistry to detect oxidisable groups (alcohols, aldehydes). Excess strong oxidiser will go all the way to acid; mild conditions (PCC, DIBAL-H) stop at aldehyde. Industrial breath analysers historically used these colour changes (now electrochemical).
